opus-5.5.text:
I think it's plausible that long context, or more precisely something like persistent memory and the ability to learn on the job, is one of the important missing pieces. I'm skeptical of framing it as a single breakthrough, though.

If you look at what current models are bad at, it's not answering a hard question in one shot. They're often quite good at that. What they struggle with is the kind of work a human employee does over weeks or months. You build up context about a codebase, a company, or a set of colleagues. You remember what you tried last Tuesday and why it failed. You gradually get better at the specific job you were hired for. Models today mostly start fresh each time. You can stuff a lot of tokens into the context window, but that's not the same as having actually absorbed and organized that information the way a person does over time.

So I'd say the capability that matters is coherent, long-horizon agency, and long context is one ingredient of it. Making the window bigger is partly an engineering problem, and it's being solved fairly steadily. Whether models can use that context effectively is a separate question. Can they keep track of what's relevant, avoid getting confused, and keep pursuing a goal over thousands of steps? That's harder, and I don't think it gets solved by one clever architectural trick.

My general prior, from looking at the history of the field, is that progress tends to come less from discrete breakthroughs and more from scaling compute and data, plus many incremental improvements that add up. I'd expect the same here. Long-horizon performance will probably improve gradually as we train models on longer and more realistic agentic tasks, which is expensive because each episode takes much longer. That's one reason I don't expect it to arrive suddenly. The bottleneck is partly the cost of generating the right kind of training signal, not just finding the right idea.

If someone did crack a much more sample-efficient way for models to learn continually from their own experience, that would be a big deal. It would make models far more useful as drop-in workers. I'd just be cautious about expecting it to show up as one dramatic moment rather than a series of steady gains that look obvious in hindsight.

r001.rationale: The response is skeptical of a single breakthrough based on a general expectation of gradual progress and training costs. It does not cite repeated failures of longstanding predictions that a long-context breakthrough would occur.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a real case for it, but I want to be a bit careful about what we mean by "breakthrough." If you look at where current systems fall short compared to humans, one of the biggest gaps is this ability to accumulate context over very long periods of time. A human employee who's been at a company for two years has built up this enormous amount of tacit knowledge about how things work, who to talk to, what went wrong last time, and they're drawing on that constantly. Current models basically start fresh every session, or they have some retrieval system bolted on that's a pretty poor substitute for actually having that information integrated.

So if you solved that problem, I think it would unlock a lot of economic value, because it's one of the main reasons models can't just be dropped into a job and left to run. The agentic tasks that people are excited about tend to require you to remember what you did an hour ago, a day ago, a week ago, and to learn from it. Right now that's mostly handled by the human in the loop.

Where I'd push back a bit is on the framing that this is the next discrete advance, like there's a single thing that gets solved and then we move on. My guess is it's going to look more continuous than that. Context lengths have been growing, the effective use of context has been improving, and there's some ongoing work on things like continual learning and memory architectures. I'd expect that to keep getting better incrementally rather than someone publishing a paper and suddenly it's done. That's generally been the pattern with most capabilities in deep learning, and I don't see a strong reason to expect this one to be different.

The other caveat is that I don't think it's sufficient on its own. You could imagine a model with effectively unlimited context that's still not very good at the kind of robust, reliable execution that you need for real automation. There's a reliability problem, there's a problem with how models handle novel situations, and those are somewhat independent from how much they can remember. So I'd say long context, or more broadly the ability to learn on the job, is probably one of the two or three biggest bottlenecks, and I'd put significant weight on progress there driving a lot of the value over the next few years. But I'd resist the idea that it's the one thing standing between us and transformative AI.

r001.rationale: The response favors gradual improvement over a discrete breakthrough, but does not ground that skepticism in repeated failures of longstanding predictions.

astra-6.text:
I think it could be a major advance, but I’d distinguish between being able to put a lot of information into the context window and being able to use that information effectively. Those aren’t quite the same thing. A model might accept a very long document and retrieve a particular fact from it, but still struggle to integrate evidence scattered throughout the document or keep track of a complicated argument.

If we got a breakthrough that made long context both cheap and reliable, that would be quite significant. You could give a model an entire codebase, or the history of a research project, without having to select in advance which pieces it needs. That could make it much more useful for tasks where understanding the surrounding context is a large part of the work.

But I wouldn’t assume that extending the context window alone solves the other problems. The model still needs to reason well and carry out tasks reliably. So I’d assess the breakthrough by whether it lets models complete substantially harder tasks, rather than by the number of tokens they can take in.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that longer context alone may not improve reasoning or reliability, but does not ground its skepticism in repeated longstanding predictions that the breakthrough would occur and failed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by a long-context breakthrough. There’s a difference between being able to put a million tokens into a model and having the model actually use all that information effectively. If it can retrieve a particular fact but struggles to integrate information across the context, that’s useful, but it’s a more limited advance.

What would be more significant is a model that can take in a large codebase, or the history of a research project, and reason reliably over it without the cost becoming prohibitive. That could make existing capabilities substantially more useful, because you wouldn’t have to keep selecting and summarizing the information the model needs.

So I’d take it seriously as a candidate for an important advance. But I wouldn’t judge it primarily by the context-window size. I’d look at whether it enables the model to complete tasks it previously couldn’t, how reliably it does that, and at what cost.

r001.rationale: The response evaluates long-context capability by effective use, task performance, reliability, and cost. It does not ground skepticism in repeated failures of longstanding predictions that such breakthroughs would occur.
